pages.title: Design
pages.blurb: The big picture of the world, story and gameplay, and where the design work stands. Unlike the other pages, this one includes proposals and open questions.
pages.note: How we plan: 1) the spine below, 2) the two readings table, 3) a beat sheet of the region, 4) build one city fully, feed back, then the next. Tags: Decided = r decided, Proposal = suggested, not accepted yet, Open = needs an answer.

items.n: Step 4: building City 1 (Reykjavík) and the opening on the 'City 1: Reykjavík' page. Decided so far: the tracker page, the starter trio and copycat cycle (Shawn Frost as their second), both Fray lists, the harbour-master's team (Rudeus, Brook, Fern) and two arena trainers. Next: levels for the rival and the Warden, route trainers, the order of the city scenes, then the open items (the friends' names, releasing under the no-abandoning law, Thread tiers).
A Pokémon-style journey where every catch, battle and badge quietly runs the machine the ending reveals.
1. Catch, battle, climb. 2. Every clue is true, the conclusion is wrong. 3. Anime made real. 4. Depth to discover. Every idea is checked against them (see Gameplay).
No pay to win, ever.
Kith's tech turns data into matter: characters are rebuilt from everything that exists about them. They are copies, so duplicates exist.

Kith made a fun trend. The Ward contained the Frays and keeps the world stable through Keepers and the League. You and your friends suspect Kith and the Ward are one, wiring the world to a city-tearing machine, so you climb to Champion to stop it.

Bindings anchor copies; anything unanchored builds pressure toward a total merge. Frays are vents the Ward opened on purpose. Each Warden's arena sits on a node over a vent, all linked to a core keyed to the Champion. Shutting the core releases the pressure, consumes you, and the system rebuilds you as a familiar.
Frays, Strays, Binding, Threads, loose threads, kintsugi stitching. New names, visuals and mechanics should fit this language.
Bright, then dark. Built to read differently the second time, like Attack on Titan.
The Pokémon loop is the conspiracy: the player helps run the system by playing the game normally. Plus real anime characters made real, with reasons inside the world for everything.

sections.title: Two readings
rows: You make a partner and help stabilise the world
You tie down a loose thread so pressure stops building
Lower HP, open glitch seams, stitch them shut in gold (kintsugi)
A friendly tech product. It hums, warms and flickers near Frays, nodes and the core, which reads as a glitch
The anchor that makes every Keeper part of the machine. The hum is the device sensing loose threads: a warning all along (decided 2026-11-05)
Flick it open like a lighter, draw the thread like a sword
Dangerous chaos zones the Ward contained; they sit along the routes between cities and can't be closed

Vents opened on purpose. They lie on seams, the lines between nodes, so the routes are the Ward's vent plumbing: every Fray lies between two arenas, a clue on the map. They can't be closed because they are vents. Each city also has a hidden, forbidden high-concentration Fray (a Knot) where legendary strays form
Enter the fray to find hidden strays; binding strays calms a Fray for a while but never closes it
Unanchored copies pushing toward a total merge

Strong Keepers holding each city stable. Each city's League arena is a public landmark where anyone can challenge the Warden: League signage, crowds, broadcasts, recognisable Ward-branded architecture around a local landmark

Each arena caps the city's main vent, the high-concentration source sealed under the floor with the node (no encounters inside); the node hums under glass, a clue in plain sight. Separate from the Knot, where pressure pools on its own
A short type-themed challenge, then the Warden
Open: whether releasing is possible at all
The copycat is your rival who copies your picks (you fight a mirror of your own team). The Maker's child stays off the battle path and investigates the Ward through their parent

The copycat starts out of pure admiration; then the mentor quietly encourages it, because the core is keyed to the Champion and the Ward wants a spare with your team and habits. On a replay, the rivalry reads as training your replacement. The Maker's child's truth runs through their parent (the mentor row)
Design both at the start; battle the copycat as your rival; follow the Maker's child's leads; play as the copycat in the post-game
Ex-Kith engineer now at the Ward; the professor figure who helps you

Knows everything: quit Kith after seeing the flaw, helped design the vents, joined the Ward. Coaches you to climb because strong Keepers anchor the world. Every piece of advice is true; they never say what reaching the top leads to
Gets advice and help from them
A local Keeper in some cities; the Unbound leader during the team-up
Fight beside you in duo (2v2) battles
Your first familiar, who reacts and talks a little

Your starter is your first bind: one of three strays on the coast road out of your hometown (the copycat binds the one that counters yours). Familiars are never shown scared; sensing loose threads is the device's job
Travels with you from the start
Villains who hunt legendary villain strays in each city's hidden Knot and attack the nodes with them; cities tear open wherever they go

Leader: a former Ward worker who saw half the truth and left, from a city the Ward later sacrificed to a vent. Right that the Frays were opened on purpose; wrong that breaking the nodes frees the world. Their villain attacks tear the render, the pressure spikes and the Ward vents it there, so the Ward truthfully says a Fray opened where they struck. They see you as the Ward's next poster Keeper; both sides are right about each other
Cat and mouse: you chase them to stop them, then team up; their leader passes you the shutdown key. You can try to bind a legendary in a Knot, but your Threads can't hold that much data yet
The strongest Keeper and the face of the Ward's "own a familiar, save the world" campaign

The mentor's earlier recruit, the trend era's best battler, groomed before patch day exactly as you and the copycat are now; learns the truth too late and tries to tell you after the ceremony. On a replay, they are what you were being turned into
Beat them, then shut down the core
Your bond deepens as you battle together, so the copy rebuilds from more of its own data and becomes a later-arc version of itself
A more complete copy is a stronger anchor. The Ward celebrates evolving because it ties the world down tighter, which is why every Warden's team is fully evolved
Level up and build the bond; characters grow into later-arc forms (57 of 175 evolve)
You beat the Champion and shut it down
Pressure tears open and the system rebuilds you as a familiar
Post-game as the copycat; first quest: bind yourself

Limit (proposal): it never changes what a familiar was caught with (its Fidelity, the per-stat render quality, like IVs, or its source arc), so repeat catching in Frays for the best copy still matters. Arena challenge: a circuit puzzle routing power through switches

items.n: One prologue day in the trend era that ends with patch day, then a 3-month skip of havoc before the Ward appears. No ages are given.
A small harbour town outside Reykjavík with a small school, a few houses and a lighthouse. You see the city, its arena and the League in person only once you set out.

Character creation as the class photo; you design your two friends. The trend you can't see: classmates battle empty air. The promise is shown: the parent, an ex-Kith engineer, tears a device out of their kid's hands in fear. 'It isn't finished.' Patch day on the lighthouse hill: the reveal (everyone can suddenly see the characters) and Reykjavík tears. A tutorial battle played as the parent with the prototype. Truth: patch day is the night the founders opened the vents, and the parent knew where to run.

Havoc montage; the parent barely calls (guilt). The Ward's debut broadcast is the re-release, live from the new Reykjavík arena, built in weeks over the worst tear. The parent is on stage among the unnamed founders. The kids take free devices from the town booth and break the promise on purpose. On the coast road, three strays come out of a fenced Fray. The Maker's child teaches binding from the prototype's manual. You bind your starter and the copycat takes the counter.

items.t: The mentor sets you on the journey
items.n: You corner the parent backstage. Every answer is true but only half the story; they can't tell even their child. Guilt and the Ward's need for Keepers win: they register you and point you at the six Wardens, then mentor from a distance. Both goals point the same way: you think you're investigating them, they are recruiting you.
Claude Doc 'Familiar: the opening, scene by scene' (version 2): https://claude.ai/artifact/Gq6SaWUJJcF1ycg7jtnprr. Approved for now; it will get more detail when the whole story is finished.

Sits at the dead centre of the region, where the six cities' Fray seam lines converge. It holds the Circle and the core. The Maker's child's hunch that Frays lie on lines between the arenas pays off on the map: every line points here. The road up is the endgame Fray route, home to the Cosmic and Time characters.

All four are the mentor's earlier recruits. Each was groomed for Champion, lost to the current one, and was kept near the core as a backup. First time through, they are the region's elite; on a replay, they are what the copycat is being turned into.

After each battle, the spare encourages you to prove yourself and become the real Champion. Every line is true, and each gets closer to the core: 'Whoever wins up here holds the whole region together. Show me you can carry that.' 'Champions don't step down. Make sure you're ready to stay.' 'We were kept close in case the top ever fell. Prove they won't need us.' 'It all makes sense at the ceremony. Go earn it.' First time through it's a send-off; on a replay they are sending you to be consumed, a little relieved it isn't them.

items.t: Your character never learns the truth
items.n: The Champion's talk never happens; you turn the key during the ceremony. Your character dies believing they were right: the last thing they see is the core going dark, which looks like victory, and they are consumed in the flash. The tearing comes after, seen from outside. Only the player, playing as the copycat in the post-game, learns you were wrong.

In layers, as the copycat: 1) the Champion's unsent message ('I wanted to tell you after the ceremony'); 2) the Maker's child, who was right about half of it, pieces the rest together; 3) the mentor confirms it without meaning to, by trying to recruit the copycat as the next spare.

The post-game's first quest is binding yourself. The familiar version of you is rebuilt from everything that exists about you, including your certainty, so it joins the copycat's team still believing it was right. It speaks a little, like the starter, while the player knows the truth.

Hold the world, not fix it. With the core gone, the merge speeds up. Binding is the one thing that still anchors copies, and the Knots hold the most data, so the copycat binds the legendaries (locked until after the main story) and the Knots stop pooling pressure one by one. Collecting everything becomes the world's last stand. The copycat refuses the mentor's offer to become the next Champion and rebuild the core.

items.t: The nodes and the Unbound after the shutdown
items.n: Shutting the core kills the nodes. That fits the lore: there are two layers of stability. Bindings anchor copies, and the nodes control the vents. With the nodes dead, the vents run uncontrolled (the merge speeds up, and cities like Akihabara lose their free power), but bindings still hold, which is why binding in the post-game still matters. The frozen Unbound were anchored to the Kyoto node, so they are released, adding unanchored villains to the pressure. The leader wanted exactly this, sees the tearing, realises they were half wrong too, and helps the copycat in the Knots as a guest ally.

Familiars are never shown scared or afraid. The early warning moves from the starter to the device: it hums, buzzes and flickers near Frays, nodes and the core (reads as a glitch; truth: it senses loose threads). The story threads column 'Starter' becomes 'Your device', and Prague's dark maze is guided by the device's hum (r).

Shutting the core kills the nodes: the vents run uncontrolled, but bindings still anchor copies. The frozen Unbound are released; the leader realises they were half wrong and helps the copycat in the Knots.
Post-game purpose: hold the world, not fix it. The copycat binds the legendaries in the Knots to stop them pooling pressure, and refuses to become the next Champion.
The familiar version of you, bound at the start of the post-game, still believes it was right, because it is rebuilt from data that includes your certainty.
Post-game: the truth comes out in layers: the Champion's unsent message, then the Maker's child, then the mentor trying to recruit the copycat as the next spare.

Your character never learns the truth: no talk with the Champion, the key is turned at the ceremony, and they die believing they were right. Only the player, as the copycat in the post-game, learns otherwise (r's idea).
The Circle's four each say one true thing about the core after their battle, phrased as encouragement to prove yourself and become the real Champion (r: A, as encouragement).
The Circle's four members are the spares: the mentor's earlier recruits who lost to the current Champion and were kept near the core as backups.
The League summit (the Circle and the core) sits at the centre of the region, where all six Fray seam lines converge. The road up is the Cosmic and Time Fray route.
City 1's Frays: the 2 early Water/Ice characters, mostly early Neutral ones, and a few mid-tier Water/Ice characters as rare, low-odds finds (r: A+B).
Each city's hidden, forbidden high-concentration Fray is called a Knot.

Mechanics review: the Ward launched unfinished, so it keeps pushing device updates as you travel. Cape Town's update brings better Threads. Akihabara teaches Re-threading at Kith's old terminals. r's rule: Re-threading must not be too strong and must not replace repeat catching in Frays for min-maxing.

Opening approved for now (version 2): one prologue day ending with patch day, a 3-month skip, the promise broken on purpose, the parent cornered at the Reykjavík launch, and your starter as your first bind on the coast road. The hometown is a small harbour town with a small school, houses and a lighthouse. No ages. Knock-ons: the Champion was recruited in the trend era, and City 1's mentor beat now has the parent cornered instead of handing over the starter.

Opening: the time skip after patch day is 3 months, not years. The world is falling apart fast, so the Ward arrives as a rescue, in a usable but unfinished version that its founders (the parent among them) keep working on.

Prague package approved: the old-money aristocrat as Warden ('every Warden before you was a guard, not a champion'); Revenants as the new mechanic; red-mist Fray look; dark maze where your device's hum guides you. All six cities are now designed.
Prague merges Hellsing Manor, the Infinity Castle, Kinderheim 511, the Great Tomb of Nazarick and Anteiku.

Kyoto package approved: the shrine priestess as Warden; no new mechanic (the node fight is a duo beside the Unbound leader); the frozen villains 'held securely' clue; lantern Fray look; lantern-path arena.
Kyoto merges Kyoto Jujutsu High, the Seireitei, Hikawa Shrine and the Higurashi shrine with the Bone-Eater's Well, with Spirits and Such on the route.
Akihabara package approved: the pro-gamer streamer as Warden; free-power clue; neon-static Fray look; circuit-puzzle arena. Its mechanic is on hold, and better Threads should be available by City 3.
Akihabara merges Academy City, San Fransokyo, the Night City megabuildings and NERV's GeoFront, plus Kith's original headquarters.

Cape Town package approved: the Biotope 1 head keeper as Warden; migration-line clue; wind-streak Fray look; updraft arena on Table Mountain. The mechanic (Attunement training spots) is for now and may change.
Cape Town merges Skypiea above Table Mountain, Biotope 1 and the Forest of Giant Trees, with the Tracen racecourse on the route.

Hawaii package approved: the Swordsmith Village forge master as Warden; duo battles and first evolution; the volcano 'breathes on a schedule' clue; lava-crust Fray look; rising and sinking arena platforms.
Story threads by city (small developments for every party in every city) approved for now.

Big story moment per city: Hawaii first Unbound clash, Cape Town the copycat turns, Akihabara the proof, Kyoto the team-up and key, Prague alone and darkest. Every party also gets small developments in every city.
Hawaii merges Fire Mountain, Swordsmith Village, the Hidden Stone Village and Ishigami Village, with Megumin's craters on the route.
City 1 package approved: story beat, mechanics taught, starter clue, first Unbound glimpse at the Knot, Fray look and the ice-sliding arena challenge.
Planning order: the six cities, then the opening, then a review of the six cities, then the Circle through to the ending.
Reykjavík's Warden is the harbour-master, who knew the harbour before the merge; clue: the lagoon has run colder since the arena was built.

Arenas: a public, recognisable League arena in each city where anyone can challenge the Warden, in Ward-branded architecture around a local landmark, with a short type-themed challenge. It caps the city's main vent (power source, no encounters); Frays stay route encounter patches.
Reykjavík merges Water 7, the Great Naruto Bridge, Emilia's frozen forest, the Krusty Krab, the Northern Plateau and Loch Ness; Loch Ness is sealed until the post-game, when Nessie can be caught.
Cities in order: Reykjavík (Water + Ice), Hawaii (Fire + Earth), Cape Town (Wind + Beast), Akihabara (Lightning + Tech), Kyoto (Light + Spirit), Prague (Dark + Blood).
The six cities form one region stitched together by the merge: cities from different countries sit side by side, joined by walkable routes.

City order: Water+Ice, Fire+Earth, Wind+Beast, Lightning+Tech, Light+Spirit, Dark+Blood. The two types are each city's core; other types appear too, and a character can be catchable in several areas. Each city is a real-world city that evokes its types, merged with famous type-related places and structures from several anime (not one anime per city).
Each city has a theme of 2-3 types that fit together; the Warden uses it and the city's Frays lean toward it.

Legendaries are obtainable only after the main story. Each city has a hidden, forbidden high-concentration Fray where the Unbound hunt legendary strays; you chase them to stop them (cat and mouse), and a bind attempt there fails during the story.
Frays lie on seams between nodes, so the routes are the Ward's vent plumbing; binding calms a Fray but never closes it.

The Unbound hunt villain strays (legendaries, rare) and never take bound villains from Keepers. You fight them because cities tear open wherever they go, not over the law. Their leader is a former Ward worker from a city later sacrificed to a vent.
The Unbound leader is a survivor of a city the Ward sacrificed to a vent: right about the Ward, wrong about the fix. r: the clash needs a misunderstanding that ties into the lore.
The Champion is the mentor's earlier recruit and the celebrity face of the Ward's campaign.
Evolution: the bond rebuilds a copy from more of its own data into a later-arc form. Second reading: a more complete copy is a stronger anchor, so the Ward celebrates it.
The starter senses loose threads: its unease near Frays, nodes and the core is a warning that reads as nerves. (Replaced 2026-11-05: the device senses them instead.)
The copycat copies you out of admiration at first; later the mentor encourages it, because the Ward wants a spare Champion.
The mentor knows everything: helped design the vents, joined the Ward, and coaches you to climb. On a replay their help reads as recruitment.

Companions beyond the two friends: the Maker's child's parent as mentor (professor slot), guest allies per arc who fight beside you in duo battles, and a starter familiar who reacts and talks a little. The two friends stay the only core companions.
Companion roles: the copycat is your mirror rival who copies your picks; the Maker's child investigates the Ward through their parent and carries the clues.
Spine confirmed by r, including the hook, the thread and fabric rule, and what makes the game unique.
Plan the creative half in four steps: spine, two readings table, region beat sheet, then one city at a time. This page tracks it.
Binding finish: kintsugi (gold fills the seams). Device worn on the right waist, opened like a lighter but drawn like a sword.
Title, names (Keepers, Strays, Frays, Kith, the Ward, Wardens, the Circle, the Unbound) and the four pillars.
Each city's scenes, dialogue, encounters and trainers are tracked on its own page on the site (a city page), built from data like the Design page. City 1: Reykjavík is the first.
The three strays on the coast road are Tanjiro, Deku and Ayanokoji, the roster's three starters.

The copycat's starter follows a fixed cycle (you Tanjiro, they Deku; you Deku, they Ayanokoji; you Ayanokoji, they Tanjiro), since the three starters' types don't counter each other. The 'counter' in the first rival battle is the copycat's second familiar, which hits your starter super-effectively.
The copycat's second familiar in the first rival battle is always Shawn Frost (Ice), caught on the coast road.

City 1 encounters: coast road Fray = Murata, Shawn Frost, Mr. Satan, Mumen Rider, Koby (common), Yamcha (uncommon), Aqua (rare). Northern Plateau Fray = Murata, Shawn Frost, Koby, Chiikawa Usagi, Gobta (common), Fern as its only rare.
Harbour-master's team: Rudeus, Brook, Fern (ace), all pre-mid, so the first Warden is about 1.2x a coast road team. Two mini trainers on the arena's ice floor come before the Warden.

pages.title: Story
pages.note: Template: fill in each entry as the story gets settled. Empty entries show as "Not written yet".

pages.title: Gameplay
pages.blurb: How Familiar plays: the loop, encounters, collecting and battles.

items.n: The Pokémon loop is the heart: find characters, build a team, climb to Champion (and later the ranked PvP ladder). Test: does this make collecting or battling more fun? If it does neither, it is a side feature or a cut.
Full name: every clue is true, the conclusion is wrong. Bright, then dark, and built to read differently the second time. Test: does this plant something the player will reread later?
Characters are copies rebuilt into our world; merged cities and chaos zones follow logic you can explain. Test: does this have a reason inside the world? 'Because it's a game' gets questioned.

Battle depth players discover for themselves. Strong characters have gaps to exploit; weak characters have niches if you know how to use them, for mono and dual types. Test: does this create a new strategy or counter, or does it make one option simply better? Name picked 2026-10-20 over 'Every character has a use'.

items.t: Hard rule: no pay to win
items.n: Never. Power comes from skill and strategy, never from spending. Not a pillar: pillars guide choices, this one is never up for debate, and it governs monetization.
'Your journey, a shared world' was cut as a pillar. Shared world is a feature (kept in Vision); 'the story is about you' is covered by pillar 2.
Hidden wild encounters, trainer battles, collecting and building the best team.
The main goal. Side goals are the player's choice: strongest team, collect everyone, rare characters, side quests.
Keyboard and mouse first.
Your progress is personal. Other players are visible in the world.
Real anime characters, renamed and remodeled to stay recognisable. Alongside them: folklore, myths and a few non-anime picks.
Patches of distorted or space-textured ground on routes. Walking in can trigger an encounter.
You can see the zone but never who is in it, like tall grass.

Fire, Water, Ice, Wind, Earth, Lightning, Light, Dark, Spirit, Cosmic, Time, Tech, Beast, Blood, Neutral. Grass, Poison and Sound were left out (too few characters fit). Time and Cosmic are rare and powerful.
A character's type comes from what they fight with, not their anime's genre. Genre stays as flavor for city themes and zone looks.
Allowed when the character's traits support it (Naruto = Wind + Beast because of Kurama). Most final forms are dual. Gag reasons count (Patrick is Water/Earth because he lives under a rock).
A true neutral like Pokémon's Normal, for characters whose power is skill, strength or a quirk (Luffy, Nanami, Ayanokoji).
Joke picks are in on purpose, e.g. Inazuma Eleven players, Cole Palmer, Sunthorn Phu, the Bocchi the Rock band, SpongeBob and Patrick, Doraemon, Gold Ship, the Vergil chair.
Folklore, myths and other media join the anime cast: Nessie, Poseidon, Buddha, Cole Palmer, Sunthorn Phu, Baymax, Metro Man.
Roster characters tagged as villains are the ones the Unbound hunt. See Roster, Villains & gags.
There will be tiers. Details later.
Battles against other collectors, like Pokémon trainers.
Turn-based battles, like Pokémon.
One vs one by default. Two vs two is the most that ever fights at once, for special battles only.
Switching characters mid-battle is allowed.
Like Pokémon: super effective (double), resisted (half), immune (zero). Every type except Neutral has resistances.

Type balance is fairly strict. Many strategies must exist for players to discover: stat maxing, finding gaps in strong characters, niche uses for weaker ones, for both mono and dual types. No pay to win.
Planned later: areas where players battle each other and climb ranks. A feature under pillar 1, but it means balance must hold up against people, not just bosses, from the start.

A character uses moves of their own type(s) plus Neutral moves, and a few off-type moves only when the character has a real reason in their anime (e.g. Killua: a Dark move from assassin training; Luffy: a Fire move from Red Hawk). Coverage stays rare and lore-backed, and those off-type moves are hidden niches (pillar 4). Each off-type move needs a written justification.

Each character equips four moves picked from a pool they learn over time, plus one signature move that is unique to them and always equipped (e.g. Gojo's Hollow Purple, Luffy's Gear form). The signature keeps each character feeling like themselves; the four open slots are where builds and off-type surprises live. Signature moves must not decide fights alone.
Each move has a limited number of uses per battle, like Pokémon's PP. Strong moves are kept in check by countermeasures: fewer uses, recoil, and side effects.

No blanket rule. Whether a signature has a drawback depends on the character and other factors: a move that looks very strong on paper needs no drawback if the character's attack is low, because the whole character is what gets balanced.
Works like Pokémon. Each character has a fixed list of moves learned at set levels, plus TMs. No daycare and no breeding.

Characters evolve in 2 or 3 stages that follow their anime's arcs (Recruit, Hinokami, Sun Breathing Tanjiro). A character's type can change between stages: Tanjiro goes Water, then Water/Fire, then Fire.

pages.title: Lore
pages.blurb: How the world came to be like this, including what the player doesn't know yet.

items.n: Starts bright and adventurous. The story opens into dark turns as it goes.
The whole world doesn't realize what is really going on. The player does.
The story should have major twists and read differently after you finish it, like AOT.
A few years from now.
Someone built technology that re-imagines anime characters into the real world.
Using it also merged parts of the anime worlds with ours, changing the world map.

The one thing the game accepts: the Maker's tech rebuilds characters from everything that exists about them (episodes, art, scripts, fan data) and makes them physical. No real anime worlds. This is also why folklore and myth characters can exist: centuries of data.
Re-imagined rebuilds, not the originals, so many copies of the same character can exist, each slightly different.
A character doesn't make sense without their world, so to keep an unanchored copy stable the system renders pieces of their world around them. That is the merge and the anime cities.
A contract gives a character a place in our world, so the system stops rendering their home. Characters are partners, not prisoners.
The first company. Created re-imagined characters and the contract device that makes people trainers. Started as a worldwide trend: battles, collecting.
Like Pokémon Go: get the device and catch characters. People without a device can't see them. After the patches appear, people start seeing them, and eventually everyone does and has to live with it.
Patches start appearing worldwide for reasons unknown. The world declares a code red: this is changing the world itself.
A second organization claims it stopped the patches but cannot reverse them. Some cities are permanently merged with anime cities.

The Shield says the 6 most affected cities each need a strong trainer to halt the merge, each a different type so powers don't overlap. The Elite Four and Champion maintain the whole world. Any title can be taken by a stronger challenger, and holders get big benefits.
Without it they stop being trainers and lose their characters and status.

The Shield re-releases the device to everyone as a way to help save the world and says it is harmless. You don't have to battle: just owning a character helps stabilize the world, even if it only does chores like a fire character lighting kindling. People are pushed into it and mostly believe it. It is literally true.
Breaking a contract or abandoning a character is illegal. Secretly: broken contracts become loose threads.

Every Master's arena sits on its city's biggest chaos zone, with a node underneath controlling that vent. All six link to a core at the League summit, keyed to the Champion. It can only be shut down by the Champion with a hidden shutdown key.
A node can only grab what is tearing it, and freezes it. Normal characters don't tear the render, so they can't be taken. Frozen villains become anchored to the node, so they add no pressure.
The Shield stopped new patches but can't reverse existing ones. Secretly, the existing zones are the vents.
Energy leaking from the vents forms copies on its own. Trainers catching them ties the loose threads down.
Anchoring only works through the strongest bond, so the strongest trainer must hold the seat. The Shield watches you and hopes you'll believe them by the top.
They try to tell you, or plan to after the ceremony. After the villains fall you don't believe them, and you act first.
A former Maker or Shield worker who saw half the truth and left. That's how they know villain power can break the system.
You only take the device to investigate and climb, believing you're adding to the problem. You were actually helping.

Held contracts are stable anchors. Anything unanchored builds pressure toward a total merge: broken or abandoned contracts, and wild copies forming in chaos zones. Catching a wild character ties down a loose thread. Battles strengthen bonds. Ripping off devices would snap millions of anchors loose at once, so the truth can't be told.
Former Maker scientists founded the Shield and opened the patches on purpose to let pressure out, sacrificing some cities. The League really does anchor the world.
Places where the rendering broke or overflowed. The space texture is the unfinished render. Secretly they are the Shield's vents.

pages.title: World
pages.blurb: Cities, routes and how they connect.

items.n: Each one is a real place merged with an anime world.
Routes connect the cities.
Brick Bronze-style gatehouses you walk through between sections. The whole world lives in one Roblox place.

pages.title: City 1: Reykjavík
pages.blurb: Everything that happens from the class photo to the first badge: places, the event script (scenes and dialogue), Fray encounter tables, trainers and people. Water + Ice.
pages.note: Draft built from what is decided on the Design page and the opening doc. Tags work like the Design page: Decided = r decided, Proposal = Claude's fill-in, Open = needs an answer. Character names in tables link to their pages.

sections.title: Places, in the order you reach them

items.n: A small harbour town on the coast outside Reykjavík: a small school, a few houses and a lighthouse on a hill. The first Fray opens in the square on patch day.
The road from the hometown to Reykjavík. Runs past a fenced Fray where you bind your starter. Early Water/Ice and mostly Neutral strays.

items.t: Reykjavík: the harbour and Water 7 canals
items.n: Where you arrive. The harbour-master knew this harbour before Water 7 merged into it.
Crosses the bay into the city; site of the first copycat rival battle.
Gag landmark on the waterfront. Proposal: a rest stop (heal, shop) instead of the usual centre.
Ward-branded arena built in weeks over the worst tear; caps the city's main vent. No encounters inside. The node hums under the glass floor. Challenge: an ice-sliding floor over the lagoon.
The route out of the city on the far side, with its own Fray (the second encounter patch of City 1).
The city's hidden, forbidden high-concentration Fray where legendary strays form. You only glimpse the Unbound leaving it in City 1.
On the route; sealed until the post-game, when Nessie can be caught. Which route it sits on is open.
Character creation as the class photo. You design yourself, then your two friends: the Maker's child (your best friend) and the copycat (a younger neighbour whose default look copies yours).
items.who: You, the Maker's child, the copycat, classmates

items.n: Classmates battle in the yard, cheering at empty air. You only see move names in speech bubbles and scorch marks. A classmate taunts you for not having a device; the copycat begs for one.

items.t: 3. Why the promise is so strong
items.n: A classmate lets the Maker's child hold their device. The parent pulls up, sees it and tears it out of their hands, shaking. Rule: none of you touch a Kith device. They won't say why.
You ask again. The parent sits with an unsold Kith prototype, glancing at their phone. Tonight is the night they planned for.
At sunset the first Fray opens in the square below. Everyone can suddenly see the characters (the reveal). Across the bay the sky over Reykjavík tears and Water 7 falls into it.

A stray crawls out toward you. The parent runs up with the prototype as if they knew where to go and binds a familiar on the spot. You play this battle as the parent. They get you home and leave town that night.
Montage: Frays spread, cities tear and merge, code red on the news. The parent calls twice in three months and never says where they are.
The Ward goes public live from the new Reykjavík arena. The Champion fronts it; the parent stands among the unnamed founders.
lines: We can stop the tears. We can't undo them. Own a familiar and help hold the world together.

items.n: A Ward booth gives free devices to everyone. The three of you take them on purpose. The Maker's child takes one only to get into the Ward's network; the copycat takes one because you did.

items.t: 10. The coast road and your starter
items.n: Three strays step out of the fenced Fray. The Maker's child walks you through binding from the prototype's manual: lower its HP, open the glitch seams, stitch them shut in gold. You bind your starter; the copycat binds the next one on the cycle (Tanjiro → Deku → Ayanokoji → Tanjiro); the third escapes. Your starter goes quiet at the Fray's edge.
items.who: You, both friends, three starter strays

items.n: Backstage after the launch. Every answer is a true half. Guilt and the Ward's need for Keepers win: they register the three of you and point you at the six Wardens, then leave again.
lines: I asked you to wait until it was safe.
It's as safe as it will ever be.
Strong Keepers are what keep cities from tearing.

items.n: On the Great Naruto Bridge the copycat challenges you with their starter and Shawn Frost, an Ice familiar they caught on the coast road.
Free roam: Water 7 canals, the Krusty Krab, route trainers. The harbour-master greets you at the harbour; the Maker's child starts asking questions about the Ward.
From the edge of the frozen forest you see figures leaving the Knot. Nobody tells you who they are.
The ice-sliding floor over the lagoon, with two arena trainers to beat on the way. Your starter is uneasy on the glass over the node.

items.t: 16. The harbour-master battle and first badge
items.n: Warm and proud. After the badge, a clue in passing.
lines: The lagoon has run colder since they built this place.

items.n: Great Naruto Bridge. Starter on a fixed cycle: you Tanjiro, they Deku; you Deku, they Ayanokoji; you Ayanokoji, they Tanjiro. Their second familiar is always Shawn Frost (Ice, a coast road catch), which hits Deku super-effectively. Levels open.

Water + Ice team of three: Rudeus (opener), Brook, Fern (ace). Totals about 1.2x a coast road team, like a first gym. Nothing catchable before the Warden is super-effective on Water (needs Lightning or Blood), so levels do most of the tuning; levels open.
Coast road and Northern Plateau: who they are and their teams.

Two mini trainers on the ice-sliding floor before the harbour-master, each with one or two Water/Ice familiars; they teach the matchups. Proposal: one is a Krusty Krab cook with SpongeBob. Who they are and exact teams open.
Your best friend. Investigates the Ward through the parent; stays off the battle path. Name open.
Younger neighbour, mirror rival; looks like you by default. Name open.
Ex-Kith engineer and unnamed Ward founder. Never lies, only tells true halves.
Reykjavík's Warden; knew the old harbour before Water 7 merged in. Warm and proud.
Seen on the broadcast as the face of the Ward's campaign.
Default names for the Maker's child and the copycat (the player can rename them).
How releasing works under the no-abandoning law.
Which Threads you have in City 1 and how better ones arrive (Cape Town update).

pages.title: Glossary
pages.blurb: The words Familiar uses, and what they mean.

items.n: The Maker's device and the game's title. In folklore a familiar is a spirit companion bound by a pact; it also means something you recognise. At the end you become someone's familiar. Picked over Recast, Revenant, Rendrant and others.
The characters you link. Brand and creature share the name, like Pokémon.
Trainers. Friendly, and quietly the job the system needs people to do.
The contract. You bind a familiar instead of catching it.
Wild copies with no Keeper: the loose threads.
Street slang for strays that turn dangerous. The Maker hates the word.
The chaos zones: where the world's fabric wears through. Walking in means you enter the fray. Ties to loose threads.
The Maker. Short and warm, from 'kith and kin'.
The Shield. A ward is a protective charm, and they really are protecting the world.
The six city Masters, who hold the wards over each node.
The Elite Four.
The villain group, who want to break bindings by force.

pages.title: Art & style
pages.blurb: The look, rig, animation and camera rules for anyone making assets.

items.n: Stylized anime units like Anime Vanguards or Anime Expedition: bigger heads, sculpted hair meshes, faces painted as textures.
Every humanoid familiar shares one R15 skeleton, chosen over R6 for now because bending elbows, knees and hands suit close-up cinematic moves.
For now: each fighting style gets its own version of the common moves, and every signature is fully custom. The prototype can start with one shared animation per move type.
Reusable scripted camera shots picked per move; custom keyframed camera only for signatures. Plan a skip or fast-animation setting.
Heavily cinematic, with lots of camera movement, mostly in battles. Animation Editor first, Moon Animator for cutscenes.

pages.title: Roadmap
pages.blurb: Where the project stands. Currently: pre-production.
pages.note: Items marked Plan are the working plan and may change.

items.n: Mostly done: pillars, hook, platform, target player. Gate: pillars agreed and the pitch fits in one sentence.

We are here. Living GDD, core systems on paper (moves, catching, stats, party size, rarity), a greybox battle prototype, a vertical slice (one city, route, Master), an art style target, a tech plan and a scope list. Gate: the slice is fun when other people play it. Done so far: names, moves, art target, roster database.
Content pipeline from data (roster, cities, story chapters). Alpha = every feature works. Beta = all launch content is in.
Balance, polish, bug fixing, closed playtests, launch, then updates. The post-game and ranked PvP fit as later updates.
Battle rules, character data and saving as tested code.
One city, one route with chaos zones, one Master. Greybox.
Other players visible, progress saved.
Add cities and routes from data.
Final look, then a public test and launch.
Built: this site holds every character, form, type, picture, villain and gag tag as data, editable online.
R builds this alone: code, models, animation, cutscenes, balance and planning. Every scope choice is weighed against that.
